summary: This informational RFC reviews the privacy and security trade-offs of different ways to generate IPv6 addresses, including both standardized and non-standardized methods. It looks at which threats each method helps with, such as tracking a device across networks, and what implementers and users give up when choosing one.

plainLanguage.summary: Your home address can tell people who you are. This paper compares different ways a computer can pick its internet address, and which ones make it harder for strangers to follow you around.

questions: how do ipv6 addresses affect tracking
how do ipv6 addresses allow tracking
what is a temporary ipv6 address
why are mac based ipv6 addresses a privacy problem
what is a semantically opaque interface identifier
subtitle: A comparison of how different ways of building an IPv6 address expose a device to tracking and scanning.

tldr.problem: The interface identifier half of an IPv6 address can be built in many ways, and the oldest way, based on a hardware identifier, lets observers follow a device over time and across networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC names four attacks against hardware-identifier-based addresses (correlation, location tracking, address scanning and device-specific exploitation) and rates each address generation mechanism against them in a summary table.
tldr.outcome: Stable and temporary opaque identifiers do best, but no choice is free: varying addresses complicate network operation, and mixing in a hardware-based address can undo the benefit.

today: RFC 7721 is an Informational document, not a standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an analysis of trade-offs rather than a protocol, so it does not itself define any address generation method.

sections.title: Many Ways to Build an Address
sections.content:
With IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration, routers advertise on-link prefixes and each host generates its own Interface Identifier (IID) to complete its address. Over the years many IID techniques have been defined, both standardized and not: manual configuration, SLAAC using an IEEE 802 MAC address or EUI-64, cryptographically generated addresses, temporary ("privacy") addresses, constant semantically opaque IIDs, stable semantically opaque IIDs, DHCPv6, and several IPv4-derived schemes used by transition technologies.

Deriving the IID from a globally unique IEEE identifier was one of the earliest mechanisms. Privacy and security problems with it were found after standardization, and many later mechanisms aimed to mitigate some or all of them. This document is Informational and analyses how each technique does or does not mitigate the attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: There are lots of ways for a computer to pick the second half of its address. The oldest way uses a number stamped on the hardware, and that turned out to be easy to track.

sections.title: Stable, Temporary and Constant
sections.content:
The RFC defines its words carefully. A stable address does not vary over time within the same IPv6 link; a temporary address does. A constant IID is globally stable, so it stays the same even when the node moves to another link. A stable IID is stable within some context, for example per link, and a temporary IID varies over time. A public address is one that has been published somewhere, such as in the DNS.

The RFC points out that how stable an address is and how linkable it is to a public identifier are independent. Nothing stops a host from publishing a temporary address in the DNS, and publishing both a stable and a temporary address where they can be linked lets all activity on either be correlated.
sections.plainLanguage: A stable address is like always wearing the same name tag. A temporary one is like changing tags often. Telling people both tags are yours defeats the point.

sections.title: Four Attacks on Hardware-Based Addresses
sections.content:
The first three attacks need the attacker to learn the target's IID first, for example as a server operator, a user of the same link, a passive observer or an on-path network operator.

  • Correlation of activities over time: hardware-based IIDs last about as long as the network interface, so activity can be linked on the order of years. Frequent refreshing does not help if other long-lived identifiers such as cookies or usernames are visible.
  • Location tracking: an IID that stays constant while the prefix changes lets a server follow a mobile host. An attacker can also probe other networks for the same IID.
  • Address scanning: the 24-bit OUI plus the fixed value 0xff, 0xfe in a Modified EUI-64 IID shrinks the search space.
  • Device-specific vulnerability exploitation: such addresses leak details like the network card vendor, helping an attacker find vulnerable devices.
sections.plainLanguage: A name tag built from a serial number lets people recognise you again and again, follow you to new places, guess other tags like yours, and tell what kind of gadget you carry.

sections.title: How Each Mechanism Compares
sections.content:
Table 1 of the RFC summarises the analysis. IEEE-identifier IIDs fall to all four attacks, with tracking possible for the device lifetime. Static manual IIDs allow correlation and tracking for the address lifetime, and scanning and exploits depend on how the IID is generated. Constant semantically opaque IIDs stop scanning and device exploits but still allow correlation and tracking. Cryptographically generated addresses (CGAs) stop location tracking, scanning and exploits, with correlation lasting as long as the modifier block and public key. RFC 7217 stable opaque IIDs stop all but correlation within a single link. Temporary IIDs limit correlation to the temporary address lifetime and stop the other three.

Combining mechanisms matters. A host with both a hardware-based IID and temporary addresses stays exposed, because an attacker can probe for the hardware-based IID. Pairing a constant opaque IID with temporary addresses removes scanning and device exploits, but tracking still works. Pairing a stable opaque IID with temporary addresses removes location tracking. A host that configures but never uses a stable or constant opaque address mitigates all four threats.

For DHCPv6, temporary addresses behave like SLAAC temporary ones, while non-temporary addresses depend on the server software. Random leases are effectively stable and opaque; sequential low-byte leases enable address scans. Addresses derived from an embedded IPv4 address inherit that address's properties and are easier to scan. Teredo clients were easier to scan until 12 random bits were added, later standardized in RFC 5991.
sections.plainLanguage: Some name-tag methods hide you well, some only hide where you came from, and some give you away entirely. Wearing a secret old tag under your new one still lets people find you.

sections.title: Costs and Other Issues
sections.content:
The RFC notes that addresses which vary over time on a link make event logging, troubleshooting and enforcement of access controls and quality of service more complex. Some organizations therefore disable temporary addresses, even at the expense of reduced privacy.

It also observes that some IPv6 compliance test suites required, and might still require, support for IEEE-identifier-based IIDs, and recommends relaxing them to allow other forms that are friendlier to privacy. Some techniques, notably CGAs, may be covered by intellectual property rights that could limit implementation. Its analysis assumes prefixes are shared by a reasonably large number of nodes; if very few nodes use a prefix, the prefix itself can be used to correlate activity.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing name tags makes life harder for the people who keep the guest list, so some places stop it, which gives up some privacy.
